# Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy {.unnumbered} Two questions decide how far you can trust an AI assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files. with your code: 1. **What can it see?** Its answers are only as good as its context, and everything it sees has left your machine. 2. **What can it do?** An assistant that advises leaves you to filter every change. An agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises. that acts removes that filter, unless you put it back. By the end you will know how to give an agent the right context, keep confidential data out of it, and hand it routine work safely. *⏱ ~35 minutes* ## Part A: What can the assistant see? | Surface | Example | What it can see | Can it act? | |---|---|---|---| | Browser chat | Any chat website | What you paste | No | | Terminal agent | Claude Code | Project files, and the output of any command it runs | Yes, in your files and shell | | Session-aware IDE assistant | Posit Assistant | Your live R session and project files | Yes, in your session and files | :::{.callout-note} **Knowing versus guessing.** An assistant is only reliable about your data when it has real information: something you pasted, a file it read, or code it ran. Column names you never supplied, or a famous dataset you never mentioned (`penguins`, `mtcars`), are signs it is guessing. Check any data-specific claim against the real object. ::: ### Exercise 1: Context decides the answer :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} The same error, three levels of context (10 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Start state:** your workshop repository open in RStudio with a clean Git pane, and a browser chat open in another window. **1. Error only.** In a new browser chat, paste only this and ask "What does this error mean?": **Prompt (browser chat):** ```text Error in `mutate()`: ℹ In argument: `mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g`. Caused by error: ! object 'mass_post' not found ``` Expect a general answer: the column does not exist, perhaps a typo, check `names()`. It cannot name the right column, because it has never seen one. **2. Error plus code plus structure.** In another new chat, paste: **Prompt (browser chat):** ```text I am running this code: voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g) and getting: Error in `mutate()`: ℹ In argument: `mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g`. Caused by error: ! object 'mass_post' not found The data structure is: Rows: 72 Columns: 6 $ subject_id "V001", "V002", "V003", ... $ sex "M", "F", "M", ... $ treatment_arm "Control", "Control", ... $ mass_pre_g 28.3, 27.9, 30.1, ... $ mass_post_g 28.5, 28.0, 30.5, ... $ metabolic_rate_post 13.21, 12.84, 13.55, ... What is wrong? ``` It should name the missing `_g` suffix. **3. No paste at all.** In the R console, `usethis::edit_file("scripts/scratch_error.R")` creates and opens a scratch script. Paste in, and save: ```r library(tidyverse) library(here) voles <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv")) voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g) ``` In the project's Terminal tab, start `claude` and ask: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Why does the mutate() call in scripts/scratch_error.R fail? ``` Expect it to read the script and the CSV file (approve any request to run code), then name `mass_post_g` as the real column. Then ask "How do you know the column names?" and compare its answer with what you know it read. **You are done when** you can say which answers named the real cause, and why. Then delete the scratch file so Exercise 2 starts clean: `file.remove(here::here("scripts", "scratch_error.R"))`. **If it goes wrong:** if Claude Code cannot find the script, check you started `claude` in the project's Terminal tab and saved the file in `scripts/`. If a chat in step 2 still guesses, that is a result too: note it and move on. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Load the data and run the failing code in your R session, then ask only "Why did my last command fail?" Posit Assistant receives the names and types of the objects in your session, and can run code to inspect them, without your pasting anything. ::: :::: ::: The answer is only as good as the context, and context reaches the model by more than one route. ### Disclosure: every route out of your machine Everything an assistant sees is sent to a model provider, by four routes: :::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="Four routes by which data reach the model provider: 1, what you paste, in any tool; 2, project files the tool reads; 3, session context Posit Assistant adds, the names and types of objects but not their values; 4, the output of commands the agent runs"} ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Route 1: what you paste ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-you} Errors, output and results you paste into a chat or prompt ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} any tool ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} Model provider ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Route 2: files it reads ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} Copilot: open files. Claude Code and Posit Assistant: any project file they choose to read ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} read ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} Model provider ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Route 3: session context the IDE injects ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} Your live R session: R version, and the names and types of your objects (not their values) ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} Posit Assistant only ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} Model provider ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Route 4: output of commands it runs ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} The agent runs `Rscript` or `head data.csv`, and reads what it prints ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} Claude Code, Posit Assistant ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} Model provider ::: ::::: ::: {.dia-caption} Everything before an arrow reaches the model provider. A data file in the project may already be disclosed; for a tibble loaded in your session, its names and types are, and its values as soon as code the agent runs prints them. ::: :::::: ::::{.callout-important} ## Working with confidential data: five habits 1. **Work on a copy.** Put a synthetic or anonymised copy in the project, and run the final analysis on the real data yourself, outside the agent's folder. 2. **Know your account.** Commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise, API) are not used for model training; on Pro or Max, set `/privacy-settings`. Check your institution's approval, ethics approval and data agreements first. 3. **Deny reads of sensitive folders** in `/permissions`, for example `Read(/data/confidential/**)`. This stops Claude Code's file-reading tools; it is best effort, because R or shell commands can still read the file. 4. **Stay in Manual mode**, and refuse any command that would print records. 5. **Describe, don't show.** `names()` gives column names and `summary()` the shape of the data; `print()`, `glimpse()` and `str()` show actual values. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Background: tool-specific notes There is no `.claudeignore` file, and `/sandbox` is not available on native Windows. Posit Assistant blocks `.Renviron` and `.env` by default, and shares the names and types of objects in your session, not their values; code it runs can still print values. ::: :::: ### Context you hold in your head A data file supplies column names, but not your question or your design. Your instructor may show this with two prompts; the demonstration is below, and you can try it yourself in *Going further*. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Instructor: demonstration Your instructor asks a new chat: **Prompt (browser chat):** ```text I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it? ``` and then, in another new chat: **Prompt (browser chat):** ```text I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading. My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to control, and whether the effect differs between sexes. The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity? ``` The first gets a tour of options; the second can get a recommendation, because the design now exists outside your head. Treat it as a proposal to check: the primary analysis is your decision. ::: ## Part B: What can the assistant do? The model is the same at every level below. What changes is its permission modeThe setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).: what it may do without asking. Each level is a rungOne level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened. on an autonomy ladder. From rung 3 up, what changes is which tool calls run without your approval. The self-study page [Build your own agent in R](11k-build-an-agent.qmd) shows that approval step in code. | Rung | What happens | Claude Code | Posit Assistant | |---|---|---|---| | 0. Suggest | Completes the line you are typing | — | Next Edit Suggestions | | 1. Ask | Answers; changes nothing | — (use a chat window) | Ask mode (`/ask`) | | 2. Plan | Proposes steps; changes nothing until you approve | `/plan` | `/plan` | | 3. Act, with approval | Edits files and runs commands, asking first | Manual (`default`): the workshop's starting mode | Normal mode | | 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Some actions without asking | `acceptEdits`; `auto` (a classifier approves actions; Claude Code's own default since v2.1.283) | Auto mode (`/auto`) | | 5. Act, unsupervised | No prompts | `bypassPermissions` | YOLO mode (`/yolo`) | **Your starting mode.** Your workshop repository starts Claude Code in **Manual**, although its own default is `auto` since v2.1.283; keep Manual for confidential data. Claude Code has no ask mode, and `/plan` can still run commands, so read any it proposes. Use rungs 0 to 3 only; the [quick reference](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd#cc-quick-reference) has the rest. **Rung 3 is where routine work is safe**, for example adding a derived column and a plot script. Three things make it safe: you start from a commit, so any change can be reverted; every edit and command is shown to you first; and a test checks the result, whatever the agent reports. Exercise 2 is exactly this. :::{.callout-warning} **Each rung up removes a moment when you would have seen the action.** `acceptEdits` also auto-approves file commands such as `cp` and `mv`, so a `cp` over a raw data file needs no approval. `auto` suits routine work you will test anyway, not confidential data or anything unprotected. And an approval you click through without reading is rung 5 with extra steps: [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) covers the rules that hold however tired you are. ::: The higher the rung, the more an agent acts on its guesses about your conventions, which is why [Block 5](11e-instructions-skills.qmd) writes them down. :::{#safe-recipe .callout-note} ## The safe vibe-coding recipe 1. **Commit**, so you start from a clean Git pane. 2. **Protect the inputs:** `/permissions` shows the deny rules, or you add one. 3. **Have the checks ready:** tests in `tests/` before the agent starts. 4. **Ask** in one prompt or skill, in Manual mode, reading each approval. 5. **Run the checks:** the test suite in a fresh R session. 6. **Read the diff** in the Git pane, then commit or revert. You will use these six steps in Blocks 7 and 9; the template ships the protections and the tests, so most of it is checking they are there. ::: ### Exercise 2: The same task, rising autonomy :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Ask, plan, act (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Start state:** your workshop repository on `main`, committed and clean (the Git pane shows no changed files). While Claude Code runs in the Terminal tab, check its work from the R console and the Git pane ([checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work)). **1. Plan a question (rung 2).** Claude Code has no Ask mode, so start `claude` in the Terminal tab and put `/plan` before your question, so nothing changes: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, how would I add a column mass_change_g equal to mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g? ``` The Git pane should still show no changed files. **2. Plan a change (rung 2).** Give a goal that spans several files: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text /plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a derived mass_change_g column (mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g). Create a new script scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R that plots mass_change_g by treatment_arm and saves the figure to outputs/ with ggsave(). Then check that both scripts run in a fresh R session. ``` Before approving, check the plan names every file it will touch, leaves raw data alone, saves the figure to `outputs/` and says how it will check the scripts run. Ask for changes if anything is missing. **3. Act, with approval (rung 3).** Choose **Yes, manually approve edits**, so it stays in Manual mode. Read each approval prompt, and refuse at least one action: if nothing is out of scope, refuse its first `Rscript` call. You will run the check yourself in a fresh session in step 4, so you see the evidence rather than its claim. **4. Review and check.** Click **Diff** in the Git pane for each changed file and read it as you would a colleague's work. Then Restart R (*Session → Restart R*) and run: **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_explore.R")) ``` ::: One test checks `mass_change_g` really is post minus pre; the other runs the plot script in a fresh R session and checks a figure arrived in `outputs/`. **5. Start your AI-use log.** Create `docs/ai-log.md` (`usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")`) and write the first line of your AI-use logA record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README. yourself, on one line, in the form from Block 1. Use today's date, written as YYYY-MM-DD: ```text 2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); added mass_change_g and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff; rejected one out-of-scope edit ``` Commit it with the agent's changes. You will add a line after each block in which an agent works; `tests/test_ai_log.R` checks that each line has four parts separated by semicolons, and that the dates are real and in order. **You are done when** both tests pass, you have read every line of the diff, and your first AI-use log line is committed. **If it goes wrong:** select the unwanted change in the Git pane and click **Revert**, then ask again more clearly. If you run out of time, the `block5-done` checkpoint branch has this block's files; switch to it from the Git pane's branch menu at the end of Block 5 if you are still behind. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Stretch: reflect on the rungs At which rung did you decide the most? Where would you have missed an unwanted change without the diff? **Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you automate this again? ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Use Ask mode (`/ask`) for step 1, `/plan` for step 2, and Normal mode (`/normal`) for step 3. Step 4 is the same: the Git pane and the R console. ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## At the command line The same checks from a terminal (after `/exit`, or in a second Terminal tab): `git status`, `git diff`, and `Rscript -e "testthat::test_file('tests/test_explore.R')"`. ::: :::: ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** hand an agent a routine multi-file change at rung 3, **trusted because** you read every diff and a test you did not write checks the result. - **Check:** the Git pane's diff after every agent action; the agent's report that something "still runs" is a claim until a test confirms it. - **Reproduce:** work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change is a diff you can inspect or revert. - **Record:** your AI-use log starts here, in `docs/ai-log.md`. ::: ## Check your understanding **You paste nothing, yet Claude Code names your columns correctly. How could it know them?**
**In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, what does the agent do without asking?**
**Which check still works whatever rung the agent ran at?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Access and cost Plans and prices change; check before the session. - **Claude Code** needs an Anthropic account, used through a subscription or an API key; see Anthropic's documentation for current options. - **Posit Assistant** uses Posit AI Pass or your own provider key, including an Anthropic API key. In RStudio, providers are configured in the assistant's settings. - **GitHub Copilot** bills in AI credits; check GitHub's plans page for what your plan includes. - **Your institution** may have approved some of these tools and not others. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Trusting a repository's configuration Project settings and hooks are code that runs on your machine. A cloned repository can carry its own, so trust only repositories whose configuration you have read. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## GitHub Copilot and the remote rung GitHub Copilot offers the same ladder in its own surfaces. Copilot Chat on github.com can also see files in the repository you open it from. | Rung | GitHub Copilot | |---|---| | 0. Suggest | Inline suggestions | | 1. Ask | Ask in Chat | | 2. Plan | Plan mode in the IDE | | 3. Act, with approval | Agent mode, approving each tool call | | 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Agent mode with auto-approval | | 5. Act, unsupervised | — | | 6. Act remotely | Cloud agent | Rung 6, the **Copilot cloud agent**, works on the repository on GitHub, in an environment GitHub runs. It takes a task such as an issue, works on its own branch and returns a pull request. Copilot Free includes only limited agent features; check GitHub's plans page to see whether your plan includes the cloud agent. The cloud agent appears in the *Going further* section of [Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd), where its pull request meets a review gate. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Exercise: context you hold in your head To try the demonstration above yourself, ask a new browser chat the first prompt, then another new chat the second, and compare the answers. A data file can supply column names and types, but not your scientific question or your design intent. ::: ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
agent An assistant that can read across a project's files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.
AI-use log A record written at the time of each piece of AI-assisted work, in the form: date; tool and model; task; what you kept or changed. It becomes the AI declaration in a README.
assistant Any AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course "assistant" is the general word; "agent" is used when the tool acts on your files.
permission mode The setting that decides how much Claude Code may do without asking: plan (read only), default (asks before edits and commands), acceptEdits (edits without asking) and bypassPermissions (never asks).
rung One level of the autonomy ladder in Block 4, from suggesting a line (rung 0) to acting with no prompts (rung 5). Each step up removes a moment when you would have seen an action before it happened.
````` ::: ::: ## References - Claude Code documentation: *Permission modes*, . - Posit Assistant documentation: *Getting Started*, ; *Permissions & Trust*, . - GitHub documentation: *Plans for GitHub Copilot*, .
